pos: adv. (according to love; the manner in which a liberty must be used)
etymology: From Latin caritas, costly love, through Old French charite. Paul's Greek is kata agapen, according to love — not a feeling accompanying the act but a rule governing it.
biblical_def: Romans 14 grants the strong man his liberty and then puts a rule over the use of it: “But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15). Paul does not withdraw the liberty; he says the man exercising it has stopped walking according to love, which is a judgment on the manner and not on the meat. The standard by which a liberty is measured follows at once: “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another” (Romans 14:19). Where the two collide, Paul gives the stronger brother the harder duty: “It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak” (Romans 14:21). And he shows what the rule looks like when a man applies it to himself: “Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend” (1 Corinthians 8:13). To walk charitably is to reckon a brother's conscience as a weightier thing than one's own freedom, on the ground Paul gives: Christ died for him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines charitably as in a charitable manner; with love, benevolence and kindness; with a disposition to judge favorably.
webster_full: CHARITABLY, adv. In a charitable manner; kindly; liberally; benevolently; with a disposition to think favorably.
CHARITABLE, a. Benevolent and kind; disposed to think favorably of others, and to put the best construction on their words and actions.
CHARITY, n. [L. caritas.] In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; that disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men, and to do them good.
EDIFY, v.t. [L. aedifico, to build.] To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge, faith and holiness.
OFFEND, v.t. To cause to stumble; to cause to sin or neglect duty.
scriptures: Romans 14:15
But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died.
Romans 14:19
Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Romans 14:21
It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.
1 Corinthians 8:13
Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.
corruption_summary: Charity is reduced to almsgiving on one side and to never disagreeing on the other, and Paul's rule — a costly restraint of a real liberty — is lost between them.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has narrowed to a tax category. A man gives to a charity and reckons that he has been charitable, and Romans 14:15 is asking about something he did at dinner. Paul's kata agapen governs the use of things a Christian is fully entitled to use. That is the sting: the rule bites precisely where a man is in the right, and a definition of charity that only covers his generosity with money will never reach his liberty.

The opposite reduction is more common in a congregation that prizes peace. Walking charitably is taken to mean never naming a brother's error, and Paul is doing the reverse of that in this very chapter — he calls the weak brother weak, plainly, and still orders the strong to yield to him. Romans 14:19 asks for what edifies, and what edifies sometimes wounds. Charity is not the refusal to say a hard thing; it is the refusal to use a true thing as a weapon against one for whom Christ died.
roots_summary: Greek agape (G26), self-giving love; kata agapen, according to love; oikodome (G3619), edification; skandalon (G4625), a stumbling-block.
roots_lines: Greek agape (G26) — the love that gives at cost; Romans 14:15, the rule over a liberty.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — building up; the aim by which a liberty is tested, Romans 14:19.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger of a trap, a stumbling-block; Romans 14:13.
Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve; the brother is grieved before he is destroyed.
Greek exousia (G1849) — liberty, right; 1 Corinthians 8:9, the right that must not become a stumbling-block.
usage: “Now walkest thou not charitably” — a verdict on the manner, not the meat.
“For whom Christ died” — the price that outweighs a liberty.
“I will eat no flesh while the world standeth” — the rule applied to oneself.

pos: v.i. (to go along with the lowly; to let oneself be carried away with them)
etymology: From Latin condescendere, to come down together. Paul's Greek is sunapagomenoi, being led away with — a passive, not a favour granted. The English word has since acquired a sneer the Greek does not carry.
biblical_def: Paul's command is one motion in three clauses: “Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits” (Romans 12:16). The middle clause is passive in the Greek — be carried along with the lowly — so the picture is not of a great man stooping but of a man letting himself be drawn into the company and the interests of those with no standing. He has already laid the foundation: “For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). Sober thinking about oneself is what makes low company bearable. Philippians puts the same duty as an estimate: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Philippians 2:3). And James supplies the reason a proud man cannot do it: “But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (James 4:6). The supreme instance is the Lord Jesus, who did not condescend in the English sense at all, but took the form of a servant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines condescend as to descend from the privileges of superior rank or dignity, to do some act to an inferior which strict justice does not require; to submit or yield, as to an inferior.
webster_full: CONDESCEND, v.i. [L. con and descendo, to descend.] To descend from the privileges of superior rank or dignity, to do some act to an inferior, which strict justice or the ordinary rules of civility do not require.
CONDESCEND, v.i. To recede from one's rights in negotiation, or common intercourse, to do some act, which strict justice does not require.

CONDESCENSION, n. Voluntary descent from rank, dignity or just claims; relinquishment of strict right; submission to inferiors in granting requests or performing acts which strict justice does not require.
LOWLINESS, n. Humility; humbleness of mind; freedom from pride.
CONCEIT, n. An overweening opinion of one's self; self-flattering opinion.
scriptures: Romans 12:16
Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.
Romans 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
Philippians 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
James 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
corruption_summary: The English word has soured into a sneer, so the command is heard as permission to patronize the poor rather than to be carried along with them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is in the English. To condescend now means to talk down, and a reader who brings that sense to Romans 12:16 hears Paul commanding exactly the posture Paul forbids in the next clause — be not wise in your own conceits. The Greek sunapagomenoi is passive and social: be led away along with the lowly, go where they go. The principle to recover is that the command is not about the manner of a great man's kindness but about the company he actually keeps.

Romans 12:3 supplies the diagnostic, and it is uncomfortable in a church that sorts itself by station without ever voting to. A congregation can be doctrinally exact and still arrange its friendships by income, its hospitality by usefulness, and its platform by polish. Paul's test is not whether the poor are welcome; it is whether the well-placed are carried along with them — whose table, whose trouble, whose Tuesday evening. James 4:6 explains why this is not a small matter of taste. The God who gives grace to the humble is set in active opposition to the other man.
roots_summary: Greek sunapago (G4879), to be led away with; tapeinos (G5011), lowly; tapeinophrosune (G5012), lowliness of mind.
roots_lines: Greek sunapago (G4879) — to be carried along with; passive in Romans 12:16, not a favour bestowed.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — low, of humble station; men of low estate.
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind; Philippians 2:3, the estimate that makes room for another.
Greek huperphroneo (G5252) — to think too highly; Romans 12:3, the thing forbidden.
Greek phronimos para heautois — wise in one's own conceits; Romans 12:16, quoting Proverbs 3:7.
usage: “Mind not high things” — the appetite that has to die first.
“Condescend to men of low estate” — be carried along with them, not merely kind to them.
“Be not wise in your own conceits” — the clause that forbids the modern sense of the word.

pos: adv. (with a grudging hand; in small measure, of sowing and reaping)
etymology: From spare + -ly. Paul's Greek is pheidomenos, from pheidomai, to spare, to hold back. The word is agricultural before it is moral: the farmer who keeps back seed is the figure, and the harvest answers the hand.
biblical_def: Paul states the law of the harvest without softening it: “But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). The figure is a farmer with a bag of seed. Seed held back is not saved; it is simply not planted, and no argument about thrift will make it grow. But Paul immediately forbids the use of that principle as a lever on a man's conscience: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). The measure is settled in the heart, not extracted by pressure; and what God loves is the giver, not the amount. Proverbs had already stated the paradox: “There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty” (Proverbs 11:24). And it names the Debtor who guarantees the account: “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again” (Proverbs 19:17). A sparing hand is not prudence. It is a wager that the field will not answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sparingly as in a sparing manner; frugally; not abundantly; with abstinence; and also with forbearance or caution.
webster_full: SPARINGLY, adv. Not abundantly; frugally; with parsimony.
SPARINGLY, adv. With abstinence; as, to eat or drink sparingly. Seldom; not frequently.
SPARE, v.t. To use frugally; to withhold from use; to part with without inconvenience.
BOUNTIFULLY, adv. Liberally; largely; in a bountiful manner.
GRUDGE, v.t. To give or take unwillingly; to envy one the possession of.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 9:6
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Proverbs 11:24
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
Proverbs 19:17
He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
corruption_summary: The sowing-and-reaping figure is detached from verse 7 and sold as a return on investment, and the promise of a harvest becomes a promise of money.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 9:6 is the most reliably abused verse in the prosperity preacher's kit, and the abuse always works the same way: the verse is quoted and the next verse is not. Verse 7 forbids giving of necessity, and an appeal that tells a poor man his harvest depends on the size of his gift is necessity with a microphone. It also forbids grudging, and the gift extracted by that pressure is grudging by construction. Paul's harvest in this chapter is thanksgiving to God and the supply of the saints, named in the verses that follow. It is not a yield curve.

The opposite corruption is quieter and commoner in a careful congregation. A man reads verse 7, notes that God loves a cheerful giver, observes that he does not feel cheerful, and concludes that he is excused until he does. Paul says the amount is purposed in the heart, which is a decision, not a mood. Proverbs 11:24 is blunt about where the calculating hand ends: withholding more than is meet tends to poverty. The sparing man is not the safe man in either text.
roots_summary: Greek pheidomenos (G5340), sparingly; hilaros (G2431), cheerful; eulogia (G2129), a blessing, bountifully.
roots_lines: Greek pheidomai (G5339) — to spare, hold back; the adverb of 2 Corinthians 9:6.
Greek ep eulogiais (G2129) — upon blessings, bountifully; the opposite hand in the same verse.
Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful, glad; God loves this giver, 2 Corinthians 9:7.
Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter; Proverbs 11:24, the hand that scatters and increases.
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to show favour; Proverbs 19:17, pity on the poor as a loan to the LORD.
usage: “He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly” — the field answers the hand.
“Not grudgingly, or of necessity” — the clause that forbids the pressured appeal.
“Lendeth unto the LORD” — who stands surety for the account.

pos: adj. (orphaned; left without the one who cares for you)
etymology: From comfort + -less. The Greek is orphanous — orphans. The KJV renders it comfortless because the Comforter is the subject of the whole discourse; the promise is that the disciples will not be left fatherless children in an empty house.
biblical_def: On the night He was betrayed the Lord Jesus met His disciples' dread with a promise of six words: “I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you” (John 14:18). The Greek word is orphanous, and it is exactly what they were about to be — children whose Master is taken, with no one to answer for them. He has already named the provision: “And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever” (John 14:16). Another of the same kind, and for ever, so that the second Advocate does not leave as the first must. The legacy He leaves is not a mood: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” (John 14:27). And Paul shows what the comfort is finally for: “Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” (2 Corinthians 1:4). A Christian may be bereaved, ruined, and afraid. He cannot, on this promise, be an orphan.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comfortless as without comfort; without any thing to alleviate misfortune or distress.
webster_full: COMFORTLESS, a. Without comfort; without any thing to alleviate misfortune or distress.
COMFORT, v.t. [L. conforto, to strengthen; con and fortis, strong.] To strengthen; to invigorate; to cheer or enliven. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console.
COMFORTER, n. One who administers comfort or consolation. The title of the Holy Spirit, whose office it is to comfort and support the Christian.
ORPHAN, n. [Gr. orphanos.] A child who is bereaved of father or mother, or of both.
CONSOLE, v.t. [L. consolor.] To comfort; to cheer the mind in distress or depression.
scriptures: John 14:18
I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.
John 14:16
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
John 14:27
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
2 Corinthians 1:4
Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
corruption_summary: Comfort is flattened into consolation — a soothing of feeling — when the word in both English and Greek means strengthening, and the Comforter is a Person.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster still had the old sense: to comfort is con plus fortis, to strengthen. The modern word means to soothe, and the difference is the whole doctrine. A soothed man is quieter; a strengthened man can stand. The Comforter of John 14:16 is not an atmosphere or an influence, but a Person the Father gives, who convicts of sin, guides into truth, and abides for ever. A congregation that speaks of the Spirit chiefly as a feeling it seeks in a service has exchanged the Advocate for the sensation, and will be comfortless in the older sense precisely when it most needs to stand.

John 14:27 is deliberately set against a counterfeit — not as the world giveth. The world's peace is supplied by the removal of the trouble; Christ's is given in the middle of it, on the eve of a crucifixion, to men who would scatter before morning. And 2 Corinthians 1:4 forbids the hoarding of it: the comfort is given so that it may be handed on to them which are in any trouble. Comfort received and kept was never the point.
roots_summary: Greek orphanos (G3737), orphaned; parakletos (G3875), one called alongside, Comforter; parakaleo (G3870), to comfort, exhort.
roots_lines: Greek orphanos (G3737) — bereft, fatherless; John 14:18, rendered comfortless.
Greek parakletos (G3875) — one called to another's side; Comforter, Advocate, John 14:16 and 1 John 2:1.
Greek allos (G243) — another of the same kind; why the Spirit is not a lesser substitute.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call alongside, comfort, exhort; the verb throughout 2 Corinthians 1.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace; John 14:27, His own, not the world's.
usage: “I will not leave you comfortless” — not orphaned, whatever else is taken.
“Another Comforter…for ever” — of the same kind, and He does not leave.
“Not as the world giveth” — peace given inside the trouble, not after it.

pos: adj. (personally and experimentally familiar with; of the Servant and grief)
etymology: From Old French acointier, to make known, from Latin accognitus, known. In Isaiah 53:3 it renders Hebrew yada, to know by experience — not acquaintance in the modern shallow sense but the knowledge of one who has lived with a thing.
biblical_def: The great prophecy of the Servant sets one word at the centre of His portrait: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not” (Isaiah 53:3). The Hebrew is yada, the verb of experienced knowledge; He did not study grief, He kept house with it. And the acquaintance was not His own trouble only: “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4). The griefs He was acquainted with were ours, carried. Hebrews draws the pastoral consequence for a believer at prayer: “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). And Isaiah will not let the sympathy stand alone without the substitution that makes it worth anything: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). A sympathetic Christ who did not bear sin would be a companion in ruin. This One is acquainted with grief because He carried it away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acquainted as knowing; having personal knowledge; familiar — and notes the Scripture use, acquainted with grief.
webster_full: ACQUAINTED, pp. Known; familiarly known; informed; having personal knowledge.
ACQUAINT, v.t. [Old Fr. accointer.] To make known; to make fully or intimately known; to make familiar.
ACQUAINTANCE, n. Familiar knowledge; a state of being acquainted, or of having intimate or more than slight or superficial knowledge.
GRIEF, n. [Fr. grief.] The pain of mind produced by loss, misfortune, injury or evils of any kind; sorrow; regret.
INFIRMITY, n. [L. infirmitas.] An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness. Failing; fault; foible.
scriptures: Isaiah 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
Isaiah 53:4
Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
Hebrews 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Isaiah 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 53 is reduced to a portrait of divine solidarity with the suffering, with the substitution in verse 5 treated as imagery rather than as the transaction the chapter exists to announce.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse most quoted from this chapter is verse 3, and it is often quoted alone. A Christ acquainted with grief comforts a sufferer, and He does; but Isaiah has arranged the chapter so that verse 3 cannot stand without verse 5. He was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was laid on Him. Strip that out and what remains is a fellow-sufferer, which is companionship in the pit and no ladder. The acquaintance with grief is precious exactly because of what verse 5 says He did with the grief.

The second loss is in verse 4's second half, which the church quotes least: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. Isaiah anticipates that men would look at the cross and misread it entirely — would conclude that God was against this Man for His own sake. That misreading is still the natural one, and it is the reason a sufferer so often assumes his affliction proves God's displeasure. Hebrews 4:15 answers it at the throne of grace: the High Priest who was tempted in all points is the one to come boldly to, not the one to hide from.
roots_summary: Hebrew yada (H3045), to know by experience; makob (H4341), sorrows, pains; choli (H2483), grief, sickness; Greek sumpatheo (G4834), to be touched with feeling.
roots_lines: Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know experientially; Isaiah 53:3, acquainted, not merely informed.
Hebrew choli (H2483) — sickness, grief; the burden He bore in verse 4.
Hebrew makob (H4341) — pain, sorrow; a man of sorrows.
Greek sumpatheo (G4834) — to suffer with, be touched with the feeling of; Hebrews 4:15.
Hebrew chabburah (H2250) — a stripe, a bruise; Isaiah 53:5, with his stripes we are healed.
usage: “A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” — lived with, not studied.
“We did esteem him stricken” — the misreading Isaiah predicted.
“Wounded for our transgressions” — what keeps the sympathy from being useless.

pos: adv. (beforehand; in advance of the need, of Mary's anointing)
etymology: From afore + hand, the older form of beforehand. The KJV uses it once, at Mark 14:8, of the woman who anointed Christ before the burial rather than after it — the only anointing His body would receive.
biblical_def: A woman broke an alabaster box over the Lord's head, the room called it waste, and He answered with a verdict the room had not considered: “She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying” (Mark 14:8). The praise has two parts, and both are unusual. First, the measure is her capacity, not the sum — what she could. Second, the timing is the point: she came aforehand. The women who went to the tomb with spices on the first day of the week came too late, for the body was risen; this woman is the only one who ever anointed Him, and she did it while He could receive it. He had already silenced the criticism: “And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me” (Mark 14:6). John records the same defence: “Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this” (John 12:7). And He fixed her deed in the gospel itself: “Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her” (Mark 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives aforehand as beforehand — in a state of preparation or anticipation; provided.
webster_full: AFOREHAND, adv. In time previous; by previous provision; as, he is ready aforehand.
AFOREHAND, a. Prepared; previously provided; as, to be aforehand in business.
BEFOREHAND, adv. In a state of anticipation or preoccupation; in a state of accumulation, so as that more has been received than expended.
ANOINT, v.t. To pour oil upon; to smear or rub over with oil or unctuous substances; to consecrate by unction.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
scriptures: Mark 14:8
She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.
Mark 14:6
And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me.
John 12:7
Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this.
Mark 14:9
Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.
corruption_summary: The account is read as a lesson about extravagant feeling, when the Lord's own commendation rests on a thing done in time and within a capacity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misreading is devotional rather than ideological: the story becomes a call to lavish gestures, and the two words Christ actually praised drop out. What she could sets the measure at her capacity, which rebukes both the woman who gives beyond her house's need and the man who waits until he can afford something worthier. Aforehand sets the timing. The principle to recover is that a good work has an hour, and that honour arriving after the hour is not the same gift.

Mark 14:9 makes an ordinary Christian's calculation look small. She could not stop the arrest, argue before Pilate, or carry the cross; she had one box and one evening, and the Lord put her deed inside the gospel wherever it is preached. The disciples' objection was not frivolous either — the money could have fed the poor, and Christ commands care for the poor everywhere. He does not answer by dismissing the poor. He answers that this hour would not come again, which is the whole force of aforehand.
roots_summary: Greek prolambano (G4301), to take beforehand, anticipate; muron (G3464), ointment; entaphiasmos (G1780), preparation for burial.
roots_lines: Greek prolambano (G4301) — to anticipate, do beforehand; Mark 14:8, rendered come aforehand.
Greek muron (G3464) — costly ointment; the spikenard of John 12:3.
Greek entaphiasmos (G1780) — the preparing of a body for burial; John 12:7.
Greek kalon ergon (G2570 + G2041) — a good work; Christ's own verdict on the deed, Mark 14:6.
Greek mnemosunon (G3422) — a memorial; what the deed became, Mark 14:9.
usage: “She hath done what she could” — the measure is capacity, not sum.
“Come aforehand” — the only anointing His body received.
“For a memorial of her” — set inside the gospel itself.

pos: adj. (turned away from; unwilling, of men who wanted no quarrel)
etymology: From Latin aversus, turned away, from avertere. Micah 2:8 uses it of travellers passing by securely, as men who have turned their backs on war — and who are stripped for it by their own countrymen.
biblical_def: Micah indicts Israel for a robbery committed against the peaceable: “Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war” (Micah 2:8). The victims are described by their posture — they are averse from war, turned away from it, walking the road with no expectation of trouble. That defencelessness is exactly what made them worth robbing, and the prophet notes that the robbers are my people, risen up as an enemy against their own. The pattern is laid out in the verses before: “Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand” (Micah 2:1); and “And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage” (Micah 2:2). Jeremiah names the settled version of the same disease, where a nation turns away from returning: “Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return” (Jeremiah 8:5). Aversion is morally neutral in itself. Everything depends on what a man has turned his back to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines averse as disliking; unwilling; having a repugnance of mind — literally, turned away.
webster_full: AVERSE, a. [L. aversus, from averto, to turn from.] Disliking; unwilling; having a repugnance of mind.
AVERSE, a. Literally, turned from, in manifestation of dislike.
AVERSION, n. Opposition or repugnance of mind; dislike; disinclination; reluctance.
SECURELY, adv. Without danger; safely. Without fear or apprehension; carelessly; in an unguarded state.
OPPRESS, v.t. [L. oppressus.] To burden; to overburden; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.
scriptures: Micah 2:8
Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.
Micah 2:1
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
Micah 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
Jeremiah 8:5
Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return.
corruption_summary: Aversion is treated as a virtue or a fault in itself, when Scripture judges it entirely by its object — what a man turns away from.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply thinned in English to a matter of taste, so that a reader says he is averse to conflict and means he finds it unpleasant. Micah's men averse from war are not squeamish; they are peaceable travellers who have laid aside the expectation of violence, and the prophet holds them up as innocent. The principle to recover is that turning away is an act with a direction, and the direction is the whole moral question.

Micah 2:1 shows where the robbers' aversion lay. They devised iniquity upon their beds, and in the morning they practised it because it is in the power of their hand — they had turned away from any restraint but capability. That is the modern reasoning entire: if a thing can be done and no one can stop it, it is thereby permitted. Jeremiah 8:5 gives the final form, a people who hold fast deceit and refuse to return. There is a stubbornness that is nothing but aversion to repentance, and it wears the same calm face as the traveller on the road.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn, return; betach (H983), securely, in confidence; chamad (H2530), to covet.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; the root behind both aversion and repentance.
Hebrew betach (H983) — security, confidence; Micah 2:8, they passed by securely.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet, desire; Micah 2:2, the appetite that takes fields.
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to seize, take by violence; the robbery Micah names.
Hebrew meshubah (H4878) — backsliding, turning away; Jeremiah 8:5, made perpetual.
usage: “Men averse from war” — peaceable, and robbed for it.
“Because it is in the power of their hand” — capability mistaken for permission.
“They refuse to return” — the one aversion that damns.

pos: adv. (at a distance; of friends who stand back from a sufferer)
etymology: A sailing term — from a + luff, to keep the ship's head to the windward and so away from a shore. The KJV uses it once, at Psalm 38:11, for friends keeping their distance from a man's affliction.
biblical_def: Among the catalogue of David's miseries in Psalm 38 is one that no medicine reaches: “My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off” (Psalm 38:11). The word is nautical — to hold off from a shore — and it is exact. They have not left; they are standing, in sight, at a distance he can measure. The psalm has already said why the sight is hard to bear: “For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me” (Psalm 38:4). This is affliction with sin mixed in it, and such affliction is the kind friends find easiest to watch from a distance. Psalm 88, the darkest of them, ends with the same isolation and no resolution: “Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness” (Psalm 88:18). The pattern is fulfilled at Calvary, where Luke records it in the same posture: “And all his acquaintance, and the women that followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, beholding these things” (Luke 23:49). The Man who was never once aloof from us was watched from a distance by everyone He had.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines aloof as at a distance, but within view, or at a small distance — and gives the nautical origin, to keep the ship's head to the wind.
webster_full: ALOOF, adv. At a distance, but within view, or at a small distance, in a literal sense.
ALOOF, adv. In a figurative sense, not concerned in a design; declining to take any share, implying circumspection.
LUFF, v.i. In seamen's language, to turn the head of a ship towards the wind; to sail nearer the wind.
AFAR, adv. At a distance in place; to or from a distance.
KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
scriptures: Psalm 38:11
My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.
Psalm 38:4
For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me.
Psalm 88:18
Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness.
Luke 23:49
And all his acquaintance, and the women that followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, beholding these things.
corruption_summary: Distance from a sufferer is dignified as discretion or as respecting privacy, when Scripture consistently treats it as abandonment.
corruption_paragraphs: Standing aloof always has a reason ready, and the reasons are usually decent. He needs space. The family should handle it. I would not know what to say. Psalm 38:11 records the behaviour without accepting any of the excuses, and lists it among the afflictions rather than among the kindnesses. The psalm is candid that David's trouble is partly his own doing, which is the case in which withdrawal feels most defensible and wounds most. Job's friends did better in the first seven days, sitting with him and saying nothing, than in everything they said afterward.

Psalm 88 is the rebuke to every attempt to finish such a psalm early. It ends in darkness, with no turn to praise, and God saw fit to put it in the Psalter that way. A congregation that requires its sufferers to resolve on schedule has made itself a place where the man in Psalm 88 cannot speak, and he will stand aloof next — not from want of faith, but because he has learned that his darkness is unwelcome. Luke 23:49 shows the Lord Himself watched from afar off, and He did not hold it against them; He prayed for the ones who drove the nails.
roots_summary: Hebrew neged (H5048), over against, at a distance; rachoq (H7350), far off; nega (H5061), a stroke, a plague, a sore.
roots_lines: Hebrew neged (H5048) — opposite, over against; Psalm 38:11, in sight but standing off.
Hebrew rachoq (H7350) — distant, far off; the kinsmen's position in the same verse.
Hebrew nega (H5061) — a stroke, plague, sore; the affliction they will not come near.
Hebrew machshak (H4285) — darkness; Psalm 88:18, where the acquaintance is put.
Greek makrothen (G3113) — from afar; Luke 23:49, the same distance at the cross.
usage: “Stand aloof from my sore” — present, in sight, and at a measured distance.
“Mine iniquities are gone over mine head” — the affliction friends find easiest to watch.
“Stood afar off, beholding these things” — the psalm fulfilled at the cross.

pos: v. (delayed, hung back; of Lot at the gate of Sodom)
etymology: From Middle English lengeren, to dwell, prolong, from the root of long. Genesis 19:16 renders Hebrew mahah, to hesitate, tarry. The word marks the gap between knowing a city is doomed and walking out of it.
biblical_def: The angels have told Lot that Sodom will be destroyed, he has warned his sons in law and been laughed at, and the morning has come. Then this: “And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city” (Genesis 19:16). Everything in the verse hangs on the middle clause. Lot is not dragged out because he was resolute; he is dragged out because the LORD was merciful, and the hands that saved him were not his own. The charge that follows is total: “And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Genesis 19:17). One of the party did not obey it: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). And Peter, who might have written Lot off, does not: “And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked” (2 Peter 2:7). Lot was a righteous man who lingered. Both halves of that sentence are in the Bible, and neither cancels the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines linger as to delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to hesitate; to be slow in deciding.
webster_full: LINGER, v.i. To delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to be slow.
LINGER, v.i. To hesitate; to be slow in deciding; to be in suspense.
LINGERING, ppr. Delaying; loitering; remaining long; hesitating.
DELAY, n. A putting off or deferring; procrastination; as, the delay of trial is not to be imputed to the plaintiff.
VEX, v.t. [L. vexo.] To irritate; to make angry by little provocations; to plague; to torment.
scriptures: Genesis 19:16

And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.
Genesis 19:17

And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.
Genesis 19:26
But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
2 Peter 2:7
And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:
corruption_summary: Lot is flattened into a villain or excused into a hero, and the verse's actual point — that a righteous man was saved while hesitating, by a mercy not his own — is lost either way.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 19:16 is one of the plainest statements of monergism in the Old Testament, and it is usually read as a character study. Lot lingers. The angels take him by the hand. The text supplies the reason in five words: the LORD being merciful unto him. Not Lot's decision, not his urgency, not even his obedience — a mercy that laid hold of a hesitating man and set him outside the city. Every attempt to make Lot's deliverance turn on something in Lot has to work against the grammar of the verse.

The opposite error is to use 2 Peter 2:7 to smooth Lot over. Peter calls him just and says his righteous soul was vexed, and Genesis says he sat in the gate of that city, offered his daughters at its door, lingered at its destruction, and bargained for a smaller town rather than the mountain he was sent to. Both accounts stand. A man can be genuinely justified and genuinely entangled, and the entanglement costs him his wife, his sons in law, his wealth, and the honour of his house. Christ's own comment on the episode is four words: Remember Lot's wife.
roots_summary: Hebrew mahah (H4102), to hesitate, tarry; chemlah (H2551), compassion, mercy; malat (H4422), to escape, deliver.
roots_lines: Hebrew mahah (H4102) — to linger, delay; Genesis 19:16, the verb of the whole episode.
Hebrew chemlah (H2551) — pity, compassion; the LORD being merciful unto him.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to lay hold strongly; what the angels did to his hand.
Hebrew malat (H4422) — to escape, slip away; Genesis 19:17, escape for thy life.
Greek kataponeo (G2669) — to wear down, vex; 2 Peter 2:7, Lot worn down by Sodom.
usage: “And while he lingered” — the condition he was saved in, not out of.
“The LORD being merciful unto him” — the reason, stated in the verse.
“His wife looked back” — lingering carried one step further.

pos: adj. (violent, roaring; of the wind Peter saw on the water)
etymology: From Middle English boistous, rough, coarse. Matthew 14:30 uses it of the wind that Peter saw — the KJV keeping the verb of sight, because the wind was there before he looked and it was the looking that sank him.
biblical_def: Peter had asked to come, had been told to come, and was walking. Then the account turns on a verb of sight: “But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me” (Matthew 14:30). The wind had been boisterous the whole time; nothing changed in the weather. What changed was where he was looking, and the sinking followed the seeing. What he did next was right, and it was brief: three words, and no time to compose them. “And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?” (Matthew 14:31). The hand comes first, then the rebuke; He does not make Peter tread water through a lecture. The word He had given before the walk is the word the wind was meant to test: “But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid” (Matthew 14:27). And in the earlier storm He had shown who the wind answers to: “And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm” (Matthew 8:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines boisterous as loud; roaring; violent; stormy; as a boisterous wind.
webster_full: BOISTEROUS, a. Loud; roaring; violent; stormy; as a boisterous wind.
BOISTEROUS, a. Turbulent; furious; tumultuous; noisy; as a boisterous man.
BOISTEROUSLY, adv. Violently; furiously; with loud noise; tumultuously.
TEMPEST, n. [L. tempestas.] An extensive current of wind, rushing with great velocity and violence; a storm of extreme violence.
DOUBT, v.i. To waver or fluctuate in opinion; to hesitate; to be in suspense; to be in uncertainty.
scriptures: Matthew 14:30
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
Matthew 14:31
And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
Matthew 14:27
But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
Matthew 8:26
And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
corruption_summary: The account is preached as a lesson in positive thinking — keep your eyes up and the water will hold — which mistakes the object of faith for the act of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The sermon that turns Matthew 14 into an exhortation to look away from one's problems has the picture and loses the Person. Peter did not stay up because he had achieved a mental state; he stayed up because Christ upheld him, and he went down when he transferred his confidence from the One who called him to his own estimate of the weather. Faith in this passage is not a force Peter generates. It is a look in a direction, and the direction is a Man standing on water who made the water.

The second misuse runs opposite and is common among the careful. Because Peter failed, the moral is drawn that he should never have left the boat. But Christ's rebuke is not why didst thou come; it is wherefore didst thou doubt. Eleven men stayed dry and are not commended for it. And the order of verse 31 should govern how a church treats a sinking brother: the hand goes out immediately, and the question comes after he is held.
roots_summary: Greek ischuros (G2478), strong, mighty; distazo (G1365), to waver, doubt; oligopistos (G3640), of little faith; galene (G1055), a calm.
roots_lines: Greek ischuros (G2478) — strong, violent; the wind Peter saw, rendered boisterous.
Greek distazo (G1365) — to stand in two ways, waver; Matthew 14:31, wherefore didst thou doubt.
Greek oligopistos (G3640) — of little faith; Christ's word to Peter and to the twelve.
Greek ego eimi (G1473 + G1510) — it is I; the divine self-naming behind Matthew 14:27.
Greek galene (G1055) — a calm; Matthew 8:26, the great calm at His word.
usage: “When he saw the wind boisterous” — the wind had not changed; the looking had.
“Lord, save me” — three words, and enough.
“Immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand” — the hand before the rebuke.
